title: Work Backwards
coreInsight: When a forward process compounds complexity, reversing invertible steps can expose the starting state much more directly.
targetLearnerRealization: When a forward process branches or compounds complexity, reversing the allowed operations from the known endpoint can expose the possible starts much more cleanly.
learningObjectives: Reverse a sequence of invertible operations in the opposite order.
Find every valid predecessor when a reverse step can branch.
Reject reverse candidates that violate the original rule or its constraints.
Verify each backward candidate by running the original process forward.

continuity.openingCallback: Turn an expression from a forward calculation into a trail that can be followed from its known output back to its unknown input.
closingSeeds: A reverse step may create several possible predecessors rather than one.
Restrictions from the original rule decide which backward candidates are valid.
A forward check confirms that a reconstructed start really reaches the given endpoint.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Inverse operations can be applied in the same order as the forward process.
Every output has exactly one predecessor.
A backward candidate need not be verified by running it forward.
Working backwards means algebraically rearranging every problem regardless of structure.

beats.purpose: Make forward guessing visibly unwieldy and let the known endpoint motivate a predecessor search.
beats.expectedRealization: Starting at the endpoint produces a small reverse tree whose leaves are exactly the possible starting values.
beats.transitionIn: An expression such as 100 + 16w records a calculation from an input to an output. This machine repeats a rule six times—but the input is the missing piece.
beats.transitionOut: The endpoint 1 did not point to just one earlier value. Reversing the rule exposed a small tree of candidates that forward guessing hid.
beats.whyNow: The approved number-machine problem gives a known endpoint, repeated conditional rules, and a purpose-built animation that makes the advantage of reversing visible.
beats.entryBridge: Follow the example once, then decide whether guessing answer choices forward or opening valid steps backward gives a checkable search.
beats.exitBridge: Six reverse levels lead to 64, 10, 8, and 1; each returns to 1 after six forward steps, and their sum is 83.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The machine flowchart reverses its arrows and grows into a predecessor tree.
learnerPrompts: Follow the displayed example forward. Why would guessing unknown starts be inefficient?
For an output v, why does 2v always give one possible predecessor?
When does (v - 1)/3 give another valid predecessor?
Which values appear three steps before 1?
Continue to six steps, then forward-check every leaf before adding them.
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—four starting values survive six reverse steps, and 64 + 10 + 8 + 1 = 83.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Begin at 1. Double to undo the halving route, and use (v - 1)/3 only when it produces a positive odd whole number.

steps.title: Reverse both machine doors
steps.body: If v came from an even input, that input was 2v. If v came from 3N + 1, then N = (v - 1)/3, but N must be a positive odd whole number.

steps.title: Grow every valid branch
steps.body: Six levels back from 1 leave the starts 64, 10, 8, and 1.

steps.title: Run the leaves forward
steps.body: Each of the four candidates reaches 1 in exactly six machine steps, including 1 itself through the cycle 1 → 4 → 2 → 1.

resolution.takeaway: A known endpoint can turn a sprawling forward search into a small, checkable reverse tree.

beats.purpose: Isolate the order reversal in a deterministic chain before naming the general technique.
beats.expectedRealization: The last forward operation must be undone first.
beats.transitionIn: The contest machine branched. Strip away the branching and focus on the order of the arrows.
beats.prompt: A number is increased by 7, doubled, and then decreased by 6 to display 30. What is the first backward move from 30?

visual.ariaLabel: Forward operation trail from an unknown start through add seven, multiply by two, and subtract six to reach thirty

feedback.minus-seven: Adding 7 happened first, so it will be undone last.
feedback.divide-two: Doubling was the middle step. First remove the effect of the final subtraction.
feedback.plus-six: Yes. Undo the last forward operation first.
feedback.times-two: Multiplying by 2 repeats rather than reverses the middle step.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—add 6 first because subtracting 6 was the last forward move.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Stand at 30 and ask which operation touched the number immediately before it arrived there.

visual.ariaLabel: Backward operation trail from thirty through add six, divide by two, and subtract seven to reach eleven

steps.title: Reverse the order
steps.body: Undo −6 with +6, then undo ×2 with ÷2, then undo +7 with −7.

steps.title: Check forward
steps.body: Starting at 11 gives 18, then 36, then 30.

resolution.takeaway: Reverse the operations and reverse their order.

beats.purpose: Expose that a conditional forward rule can give one output more than one valid predecessor.
beats.expectedRealization: Both an even halving route and an odd 3N + 1 route can reach the same output.
beats.transitionIn: A fixed chain has one backward trail. The number machine is different because two forward doors can meet at one output.
beats.prompt: In the number machine, an even input is halved and an odd input becomes 3N + 1. Which inputs produce 22 in one step? Select all that work.

response.feedback: Test each candidate with the original odd-or-even rule.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes—44 is halved to 22, and 7 becomes 3(7) + 1 = 22.
beats.incorrectFeedback: One predecessor comes through the even door and another may come through the odd door.

visual.ariaLabel: Two predecessor branches showing that forty-four and seven both produce twenty-two

steps.title: Open the even door
steps.body: Doubling 22 gives 44, and the machine halves that even input back to 22.

steps.title: Open the odd door
steps.body: Solving 3N + 1 = 22 gives N = 7, which is odd, so that route is allowed.

resolution.takeaway: Reversing a rule may branch; keep every predecessor that obeys the original forward condition.

beats.purpose: Show why algebraically reversing a formula is insufficient when the original rule has a condition.
beats.expectedRealization: A whole-number reverse calculation can still be invalid because the candidate would have taken a different forward door.
beats.transitionIn: The calculation (v - 1)/3 sometimes produces a whole number. That alone does not prove the odd-input door was available.
beats.prompt: Working back from output 7 gives candidates 14 and (7 − 1)/3 = 2. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Only 2 is valid because the division came out whole.
Only 14 is valid because 2 would take the even-input door.
Neither is valid because 7 is odd.

feedback.both: Run 2 through the original machine; its parity chooses the wrong door.
feedback.two-only: A whole quotient is necessary, but the original input must also be odd.
feedback.fourteen-only: Correct. The original rule sends 14 to 7 but sends 2 to 1.
feedback.neither: The output's parity does not choose the forward door; the predecessor's parity does.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct—14 → 7, while the even candidate 2 is halved to 1.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A reverse candidate is only provisional. Feed it through the original machine rule.

steps.title: Test 14
steps.body: Because 14 is even, the machine halves it.

steps.title: Test 2
steps.body: Although (7 − 1)/3 = 2 is whole, 2 is even. The machine would halve it instead of using 3N + 1.

resolution.takeaway: An inverse calculation proposes a candidate; the original rule decides whether it survives.

beats.purpose: Name the strategy after the learner has reversed order, followed branches, and rejected an invalid predecessor.
beats.expectedRealization: Working backwards reconstructs possible earlier states from a known endpoint by reversing steps and preserving constraints.
beats.transitionIn: You have followed arrows in reverse, opened every allowed predecessor branch, and checked each candidate against the forward rule.
beats.name: Work backwards
beats.conciseDefinition: Start from a known ending and reverse the process one step at a time, keeping every candidate allowed by the original rules.
beats.formalization: known endpoint → undo the last step → continue through every valid predecessor → run candidates forward to verify
beats.memoryHook: Last step first; keep valid branches; check forward.

beats.purpose: Prevent overgeneralizing the technique to problems whose structure offers no useful reverse trail.
beats.expectedRealization: Working backwards is especially useful when the endpoint is known and the intervening steps can be reversed more cleanly than starts can be guessed.
beats.transitionIn: Working backwards is a strategy, not a rule that every problem must obey. Look for a known finish and reversible steps.
beats.prompt: Which situation most strongly suggests working backwards?

options.text: The final display is known, the start is unknown, and each machine step can be reversed.
The starting value and every forward operation are already given.
A table lists favorite colors and asks for the most common one.
A rectangle's two side lengths are given and its area is requested.

feedback.finish: Exactly. The endpoint gives a foothold and the reversible steps create a path back.
feedback.evaluate: A direct forward calculation is already efficient here.
feedback.survey: Reading or tallying the table is more direct than inventing reverse steps.
feedback.area: Multiplying the given side lengths is already direct.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—a known finish plus reversible steps is the strongest signal.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Choose the situation where the ending gives useful information about earlier states.

steps.title: Compare directions
steps.body: If forward work is already a short calculation, use it. Reverse direction when the ending is known and guessing starts would create unnecessary search.

resolution.takeaway: Choose the direction that makes the chain of reasoning smaller and easier to verify.

beats.purpose: Assess a near deterministic chain with three inverses in the opposite order.
beats.expectedRealization: Undoing subtract, multiply, then add recovers 6 and a forward check returns 29.
beats.transitionIn: Start with a clean three-step trail. Write the inverse under each arrow before calculating.
beats.transitionOut: The reverse trail found 6, and the original forward trail confirmed it.
beats.whyNow: This near-transfer item checks the essential last-step-first order without branching.
beats.entryBridge: Begin at 29 and undo −4, then ×3, then +5.
beats.exitBridge: The recovered start 6 reproduces the display exactly.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The operation trail from the concept-building interaction returns as an independent problem.
learnerPrompts: What operation happened last?
What inverse undoes it?
Does the recovered start return to 30?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—29 → 33 → 11 → 6 backwards, and 6 returns to 29 forwards.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Reverse both the operations and their order: first add 4, then divide by 3, then subtract 5.

steps.title: Walk backward
steps.body: Undo the final subtraction, then the tripling, then the initial addition.

steps.title: Check forward
steps.body: The original chain sends 6 to 29.

resolution.takeaway: A deterministic chain reverses cleanly when each inverse is applied last-step-first.

beats.purpose: Assess the same inverse-order structure in a time-ordered measurement context.
beats.expectedRealization: Reversing +2, ×3, and −4 from 32 recovers the 9 a.m. count 14.
beats.transitionIn: Now the arrows are moments in time instead of symbols in a machine. The latest recorded change must still be undone first.
beats.transitionOut: Reading the log upward recovered the earlier count, and replaying it downward verified the result.
beats.whyNow: A context change tests whether the learner sees temporal order rather than relying on a familiar algebra layout.
beats.entryBridge: Start at noon and reverse the 11-to-noon change before touching the earlier changes.
beats.exitBridge: The count 14 reproduces every line of the lab log and ends at 32.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The operation trail becomes a chronological record read from bottom to top.
learnerPrompts: Which logged change happened most recently?
What inverse recovers the 11 a.m. count?
How can the complete log verify the start?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—undoing the log from noon gives 30, then 10, then 14.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Read the changes from latest to earliest: subtract 2, divide by 3, then add 4.

steps.title: Read the log backward
steps.body: Undo +2, then ×3, then −4.

steps.title: Replay the log
steps.body: Starting with 14 gives 10, then 30, then 32.

resolution.takeaway: A time sequence reverses from the latest change back to the earliest.

beats.purpose: Assess a small reverse search in which each move offers two invertible choices.
beats.expectedRealization: Two reverse levels from 20 give the four distinct starts 12, 8, 6, and 5.
beats.transitionIn: One fixed trail had one start. Let each move offer two choices and keep every backward branch.
beats.transitionOut: The four leaves cover every two-move history because each reverse level opened both allowed doors.
beats.whyNow: This mixed item transfers the predecessor-tree idea to freely chosen operations rather than a parity-controlled rule.
beats.entryBridge: From 20, undo +4 and ×2. Repeat both reverse moves from every value one level earlier.
beats.exitBridge: The distinct starts 12, 8, 6, and 5 each reach 20 through an allowed two-move route.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The contest predecessor tree is rebuilt with two always-open inverse doors.
learnerPrompts: What values can be one move before 20?
What values can be one move before each of those?
Are any leaves duplicated?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—12, 8, 6, and 5 are the four distinct positive starts.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Work back two complete levels: replace +4 by −4 and ×2 by ÷2 at every node.

visual.ariaLabel: Two-level reverse tree from twenty through sixteen and ten to starts twelve, eight, six, and five

steps.title: One move back
steps.body: Before 20, the number was 16 if +4 was used or 10 if ×2 was used.

steps.title: Two moves back
steps.body: Before 16, the starts were 12 or 8. Before 10, they were 6 or 5. All four are positive and distinct.

steps.title: Verify coverage
steps.body: 12 → 16 → 20, 8 → 16 → 20, 6 → 10 → 20, and 5 → 10 → 20 use exactly two allowed moves.

resolution.takeaway: When several operations are allowed, reverse every allowed door at every level and merge duplicates if they occur.

beats.purpose: Transfer reverse-order reasoning to changes in a real quantity and require a forward audit.
beats.expectedRealization: Undoing use, duplication, and giveaway recovers an original stock of 18 stickers.
beats.transitionIn: A written record can hide its starting quantity just as a machine does. Use the final inventory as the foothold.
beats.transitionOut: The recovered stock is trustworthy because replaying all three events returns to the recorded final count.
beats.whyNow: This mixed context checks that the strategy follows causal order without relying on explicit machine arrows.
beats.entryBridge: Begin with the final 17 and reverse the last use, the duplication, and the first giveaway.
beats.exitBridge: Starting with 18, the recorded events produce 11, then 22, then 17 stickers.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The chronological log from the prior item becomes an inventory record with reversible events.
learnerPrompts: What count existed just before five stickers were used?
What count existed before the remaining collection doubled?
Does the reconstructed start replay correctly?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Undo using five by adding five, undo doubling by halving, then undo giving away seven by adding seven.

steps.title: Reverse the record
steps.body: Before five were used there were 22; before the collection doubled there were 11; before seven were given away there were 18.

steps.title: Replay every event
steps.body: Beginning with 18: give away 7 to leave 11, double to 22, then use 5 to leave 17.

resolution.takeaway: Working backwards reconstructs the start; replaying the story checks that each event kept its meaning.

beats.purpose: Assess a constrained three-level predecessor tree with invalid branches and multiple verified leaves.
beats.expectedRealization: Reversing the parity rule from 4 for three steps yields exactly 32, 11, and 6, whose sum is 49.
beats.transitionIn: Finish with a conditional machine. Some inverse calculations will fail, so every proposed branch must earn its place.
beats.transitionOut: The final leaves survived both the backward conditions and an exact three-step forward check.
beats.whyNow: This challenge combines inverse order, branching, rule restrictions, exact step count, and verification without copying the mapped machine's numbers.
beats.entryBridge: From each output v, try 2v and v − 5. Keep v − 5 only when it is a positive odd input to the +5 door.
beats.exitBridge: The valid leaves 32, 11, and 6 all reach 4 in exactly three steps and sum to 49.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The authentic parity-controlled predecessor tree returns with a different odd rule and target.
learnerPrompts: What can produce 4 in one step?
At which output does the odd-input branch first open?
Which three-step starts survive a forward check?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—the three valid starts are 32, 11, and 6, with sum 49.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Grow three reverse levels from 4. The v − 5 branch works only when it is positive and odd.

visual.ariaLabel: Three-level reverse tree from four to valid starts thirty-two, eleven, and six

steps.title: First level
steps.body: Only 8 precedes 4: 8 is even and halves to 4. The other inverse, 4 − 5, is negative.

steps.title: Second level
steps.body: Both 16 and 3 precede 8: 16 halves to 8, while odd 3 increases by 5 to 8.

steps.title: Third level
steps.body: The predecessors of 16 are 32 and odd 11. The only predecessor of 3 is 6. Thus the leaves are 32, 11, and 6.

resolution.takeaway: A complete backward tree opens every legal branch, rejects illegal ones, and verifies every surviving leaf.

beats.purpose: Consolidate the full strategy, including when to use it and how to validate its result.
beats.expectedRealization: A reliable reverse solution needs a useful endpoint, opposite-order inverses, complete valid branching, and a forward check.
beats.transitionIn: Operation trails, logs, inventories, and machines all used the same safeguards. Gather them into one checklist.
beats.prompt: Which checks belong in a reliable work-backwards solution? Select all four.

options.text: Start from a known endpoint that gives useful information.
Undo the last forward step first.
Keep every reverse branch allowed by the original rules.
Run each surviving candidate forward to verify it.
Assume every endpoint has exactly one predecessor.

response.feedback: Think about direction, inverse order, completeness, and verification.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—use the endpoint, reverse the order, preserve every valid branch, and check forward.
beats.incorrectFeedback: An endpoint can have several predecessors. Keep the other four safeguards.

visual.ariaLabel: Four checks for a reliable work-backwards solution

steps.body: A known ending gives the search a foothold.
Inverse steps are taken in the reverse of the forward order.
Original conditions control which branches survive, and a forward replay confirms the result.

resolution.takeaway: Last step first; keep valid branches; check forward.

beats.purpose: Leave a precise question about non-invertible steps and extra constraints after consolidating the core strategy.
beats.expectedRealization: Some operations erase information, so reversing them may require multiple candidates or an additional condition.
beats.transitionIn: Every reverse branch so far came from a rule we could state exactly. Now let one step erase a sign.
beats.prompt: A machine squares its input and displays 9. Working backwards suggests both 3 and −3. What extra information could make the starting value unique?
beats.takeaway: When a forward step loses information, working backwards produces candidates; an original constraint must decide among them.

notes: Draft technique lesson authored from the approved S1 compact context packet.
The approved AMC 8 2020 Problem 22 is the discovery anchor and uses the existing reverse-machine animation as a complete controlled timeline.
Generated practice separates deterministic inverse chains, freely branching operations, and constrained predecessor trees.
All generated answers and choices were recomputed with an independent forward replay or exhaustive reverse-tree audit.
All visuals reuse generic declarative primitives; no lesson-specific renderer branch was added.
